source_concept: Prepare the Organization — Define Security Requirements for Software Development
proposed_assessment_use: Use as an interview and artifact prompt for how development security requirements are established, maintained, and communicated.
evidence_examples: security requirements; engineering standards; exception records; review checklists
adaptation_limit: A practice reference, not proof that a team follows it and not a compliance criterion.

source_concept: Prepare the Organization — Implement Roles and Responsibilities
proposed_assessment_use: Test whether security responsibilities, decision rights, and escalation paths are explicit across delivery roles.
evidence_examples: RACI or role definitions; onboarding material; review ownership; escalation records
adaptation_limit: Role clarity must be observed in the assessed team; publication of a role model alone is intent evidence.

source_concept: Prepare the Organization — Implement Supporting Toolchains
proposed_assessment_use: Ask how toolchains support security practices consistently from source through build and delivery.
evidence_examples: repository controls; CI/CD configuration; scanning integrations; build provenance
adaptation_limit: Tool presence is not equivalent to effective use; configuration, coverage, and response evidence are separate.

source_concept: Prepare the Organization — Define and Use Criteria for Software Security Checks
proposed_assessment_use: Assess whether teams define release or change criteria for security checks and how exceptions are handled.
evidence_examples: quality gates; scan thresholds; waiver criteria; release checklists
adaptation_limit: Do not impose one universal threshold across ESS, RIS, and IAM; criteria should be interpreted in local risk context.

source_concept: Prepare the Organization — Implement and Maintain Secure Environments for Software Development
proposed_assessment_use: Examine separation, access, maintenance, and monitoring of development/build environments.
evidence_examples: environment inventory; access controls; CI runner configuration; maintenance records
adaptation_limit: This does not prescribe a specific hosting model or vendor.

source_concept: Protect the Software — Protect All Forms of Code from Unauthorized Access and Tampering
proposed_assessment_use: Check how source and related code artifacts are protected through least privilege and change controls.
evidence_examples: repository permissions; branch protections; access reviews; audit logs
adaptation_limit: Controls must be sampled in the actual repositories or systems in scope; policy alone is not implementation evidence.

source_concept: Protect the Software — Provide a Mechanism for Verifying Software Release Integrity
proposed_assessment_use: Ask how release integrity is established and verified before or during deployment.
evidence_examples: signatures; checksums; provenance records; controlled artifact repositories
adaptation_limit: Mechanisms vary by delivery model; absence of one named technique is not itself a finding.

source_concept: Protect the Software — Archive and Protect Each Software Release
proposed_assessment_use: Assess whether released artifacts and supporting provenance can be reconstructed for investigation and rollback.
evidence_examples: release archives; manifests; retained build metadata; rollback records
adaptation_limit: Retention needs depend on service and University policy; the SSDF practice is not a retention schedule.

source_concept: Produce Well-Secured Software — Design Software to Meet Security Requirements and Mitigate Security Risks
proposed_assessment_use: Test how security requirements and risk analysis influence design decisions before implementation.
evidence_examples: architecture decisions; threat models; design reviews; risk records
adaptation_limit: Use to structure evidence collection, not to infer that every change requires the same design ceremony.

source_concept: Produce Well-Secured Software — Review the Software Design
proposed_assessment_use: Assess whether design review checks alignment with requirements and identified risk.
evidence_examples: design-review records; architecture review notes; security sign-off; exception logs
adaptation_limit: Review depth should be calibrated to risk and change type; no maturity score is implied.

source_concept: Produce Well-Secured Software — Reuse Existing, Well-Secured Software When Feasible
proposed_assessment_use: Explore dependency selection, reuse decisions, and evaluation of external components.
evidence_examples: dependency inventories; component approval criteria; upgrade records; SBOMs where used
adaptation_limit: This is not a procurement recommendation and does not require any particular component-management product.

source_concept: Produce Well-Secured Software — Create Source Code by Adhering to Secure Coding Practices
proposed_assessment_use: Assess how secure coding expectations are translated into day-to-day development and review.
evidence_examples: coding standards; review templates; training; defect examples
adaptation_limit: Published standards are intent evidence until implementation is corroborated.

source_concept: Produce Well-Secured Software — Configure Compilation, Interpreter, and Build Processes to Improve Executable Security
proposed_assessment_use: Inspect repeatability and security-relevant configuration of build processes.
evidence_examples: build definitions; compiler/interpreter settings; immutable pipeline definitions; build logs
adaptation_limit: Applicability differs for compiled, interpreted, low-code, SaaS, and vendor-managed systems.

source_concept: Produce Well-Secured Software — Review and/or Analyze Human-Readable Code
proposed_assessment_use: Examine review and analysis practices used to find vulnerabilities and verify requirements.
evidence_examples: peer-review records; static analysis; review coverage; remediation evidence
adaptation_limit: Tool output counts as detection evidence only when scope, triage, and disposition are known.

source_concept: Produce Well-Secured Software — Test Executable Code
proposed_assessment_use: Assess executable testing used to identify vulnerabilities and verify security requirements.
evidence_examples: dynamic testing; integration tests; security test plans; findings and fixes
adaptation_limit: Specific testing techniques should be selected by context; this crosswalk does not require a particular tool.

source_concept: Produce Well-Secured Software — Configure Software to Have Secure Settings by Default
proposed_assessment_use: Ask how secure defaults, deployment configuration, and documented exceptions are maintained.
evidence_examples: configuration baselines; deployment templates; hardening standards; exception records
adaptation_limit: Secure-default evidence must be interpreted against the service's actual operational context.

source_concept: Respond to Vulnerabilities — Identify and Confirm Vulnerabilities on an Ongoing Basis
proposed_assessment_use: Examine intake, monitoring, confirmation, and disclosure paths for vulnerabilities affecting delivered software.
evidence_examples: vulnerability intake; disclosure process; monitoring feeds; triage records
adaptation_limit: Volume of findings alone is not a performance or maturity measure.

source_concept: Respond to Vulnerabilities — Assess, Prioritize, and Remediate Vulnerabilities
proposed_assessment_use: Assess prioritization logic, ownership, remediation tracking, and risk acceptance.
evidence_examples: severity criteria; remediation SLAs or objectives; tickets; exceptions; verification
adaptation_limit: Do not compare raw remediation times without severity, service criticality, and denominator context.

source_concept: Respond to Vulnerabilities — Analyze Vulnerabilities to Identify Their Root Causes
proposed_assessment_use: Look for learning loops that translate vulnerability root causes into process or design changes.
evidence_examples: root-cause analyses; recurring-defect trends; revised controls; retrospective actions
adaptation_limit: A single retrospective is not evidence of a sustained learning system.

source_concept: GOVERN — Organizational Context
proposed_assessment_use: Frame mission, stakeholder, dependency, and service-context questions before interpreting cybersecurity practices.
evidence_examples: service charters; stakeholder maps; dependency registers; critical-service definitions
adaptation_limit: CSF outcomes are high-level and non-prescriptive; they are not direct evidence of Iowa practice.

source_concept: GOVERN — Risk Management Strategy
proposed_assessment_use: Assess how priorities, constraints, risk tolerance, and assumptions guide operational risk decisions.
evidence_examples: risk criteria; exception rules; prioritization records; decision logs
adaptation_limit: Do not translate risk language into an invented maturity score.

source_concept: GOVERN — Roles, Responsibilities, and Authorities
proposed_assessment_use: Map accountability and decision rights across central IT, ESS, RIS, IAM, and shared services.
evidence_examples: role matrices; escalation paths; ownership records; governance charters
adaptation_limit: Formal assignment is intent evidence until corroborated in operating records and interviews.

source_concept: GOVERN — Policy
proposed_assessment_use: Compare policy expectations with sampled implementation evidence and exception handling.
evidence_examples: policies; standards; exception records; implementation samples
adaptation_limit: This engagement is not a compliance audit; policy-to-practice differences require contextual interpretation.

source_concept: GOVERN — Oversight
proposed_assessment_use: Assess review cadences and feedback loops used to oversee cybersecurity risk management.
evidence_examples: governance minutes; risk reviews; dashboard definitions; action tracking
adaptation_limit: Oversight frequency alone is not an outcome measure.

source_concept: GOVERN — Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management
proposed_assessment_use: Explore governance of third-party software, services, and dependencies where relevant to assessed systems.
evidence_examples: vendor/dependency inventories; review criteria; contract controls; risk records
adaptation_limit: Use for operating-practice questions only; the RFQ excludes procurement recommendations.

source_concept: IDENTIFY — Asset Management
proposed_assessment_use: Assess whether hardware, software, services, systems, and data relevant to the services are known and lifecycle-managed.
evidence_examples: service inventory; application catalog; data inventory; ownership metadata
adaptation_limit: Inventory completeness must be tested against defined scope; no universal asset taxonomy is imposed.

source_concept: IDENTIFY — Risk Assessment
proposed_assessment_use: Examine identification and prioritization of vulnerabilities, threats, impacts, and risk responses.
evidence_examples: risk assessments; vulnerability records; threat analyses; exception decisions
adaptation_limit: Raw finding counts are not comparable across groups without common scope and denominator.

source_concept: IDENTIFY — Improvement
proposed_assessment_use: Look for lessons learned and continuous improvement from evaluations, tests, exercises, and incidents.
evidence_examples: retrospectives; corrective-action tracking; policy/process revisions; exercise results
adaptation_limit: Presence of a backlog is not evidence that improvement actions close effectively.

source_concept: PROTECT — Identity Management, Authentication, and Access Control
proposed_assessment_use: Structure IAM discovery around identity lifecycle, authentication, authorization, and access governance outcomes.
evidence_examples: joiner/mover/leaver records; access reviews; MFA policy and samples; privileged-access controls
adaptation_limit: Do not infer architecture or product choices from the CSF category.

source_concept: PROTECT — Awareness and Training
proposed_assessment_use: Ask how role-relevant security knowledge is maintained for practitioners and service operators.
evidence_examples: training curricula; completion records; role-specific exercises; onboarding
adaptation_limit: Completion percentage is not equivalent to behavior change or security outcome.

source_concept: PROTECT — Data Security
proposed_assessment_use: Assess safeguards for confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data in the assessed service context.
evidence_examples: data classifications; encryption configurations; backup controls; transfer rules
adaptation_limit: Data handling expectations must be reconciled with University policy and actual system boundaries.

source_concept: PROTECT — Platform Security
proposed_assessment_use: Examine configuration, maintenance, software integrity, and change controls for platforms supporting services.
evidence_examples: configuration baselines; patch records; change records; platform inventories
adaptation_limit: Applicability differs for University-managed and externally managed platforms.

source_concept: PROTECT — Technology Infrastructure Resilience
proposed_assessment_use: Assess whether service architecture and operational safeguards support resilience objectives.
evidence_examples: redundancy design; backup/restore evidence; capacity planning; continuity controls
adaptation_limit: Do not assert resilience from architecture diagrams alone; operating evidence is required.

source_concept: DETECT — Continuous Monitoring
proposed_assessment_use: Assess monitoring coverage and how telemetry supports detection across relevant runtime environments.
evidence_examples: monitoring inventory; alert rules; coverage maps; alert samples
adaptation_limit: Alert volume is not a quality metric without coverage, precision, and response context.

source_concept: DETECT — Adverse Event Analysis
proposed_assessment_use: Examine how events are analyzed, correlated, escalated, and contextualized.
evidence_examples: event triage records; correlation logic; escalation criteria; incident linkage
adaptation_limit: Detection capability cannot be inferred solely from tool deployment.

source_concept: RESPOND — Incident Management
proposed_assessment_use: Assess declaration, coordination, prioritization, and closure practices for incidents.
evidence_examples: incident procedures; severity model; incident tickets; coordination records
adaptation_limit: Incident count must not be treated as a maturity ranking; reporting culture and service scale matter.

source_concept: RESPOND — Incident Analysis
proposed_assessment_use: Assess analysis quality, evidence preservation, root cause, and learning from incidents.
evidence_examples: timelines; root-cause analyses; forensic records; follow-up actions
adaptation_limit: Depth of analysis should be calibrated to incident significance and available evidence.

source_concept: RESPOND — Incident Response Reporting and Communication
proposed_assessment_use: Map internal and stakeholder communication expectations during incidents.
evidence_examples: communication plans; notification records; role/contact maps; post-incident communications
adaptation_limit: The crosswalk does not define legal notification obligations.

source_concept: RESPOND — Incident Mitigation
proposed_assessment_use: Assess how incidents are contained and eradicated while managing service impact.
evidence_examples: containment procedures; remediation records; emergency changes; validation evidence
adaptation_limit: Containment speed should not be compared without incident type, severity, and service context.

source_concept: RECOVER — Incident Recovery Plan Execution
proposed_assessment_use: Assess restoration priorities, recovery execution, validation, and transition back to normal operations.
evidence_examples: recovery plans; restore tests; recovery timelines; validation records
adaptation_limit: A documented plan is intent evidence until exercised or demonstrated.

source_concept: RECOVER — Incident Recovery Communication
proposed_assessment_use: Assess stakeholder coordination and status communication during recovery.
evidence_examples: recovery communications; stakeholder lists; status updates; closure messages
adaptation_limit: Communication quality should be evaluated in context, not by message volume.

source_concept: Organizational Profiles
proposed_assessment_use: Use Current/Target Profile concepts as a neutral way to organize observed and desired outcomes and gap actions.
evidence_examples: current-state evidence; target-state decisions; gap/action register
adaptation_limit: Profiles organize outcomes; they do not create an empirical benchmark or universal maturity level.

source_concept: CSF Tiers
proposed_assessment_use: Use only as contextual vocabulary for rigor of risk governance and management if the University finds it useful.
evidence_examples: governance characteristics; risk-management practices; stakeholder context
adaptation_limit: Do not convert Tiers into a TJLabs maturity score, percentile, certification, or cross-team ranking; NIST presents them as contextual characterization that complements risk-management methodology.

source_concept: Policies, processes, procedures, and practices are reviewed regularly and updated as needed
proposed_assessment_use: Ask whether AI-related governance is periodically reviewed as technologies, uses, and risks change.
evidence_examples: governance review records; policy revision history; decision logs
adaptation_limit: Apply only where AI use is actually in scope; public AI policy does not establish ESS/RIS/IAM adoption.

source_concept: Mechanisms inventory AI systems and are resourced according to organizational risk priorities
proposed_assessment_use: Assess whether the organization can identify AI systems/use cases in scope and assign accountable resources.
evidence_examples: AI use-case inventory; ownership; risk classification; lifecycle status
adaptation_limit: Inventory design is organization-specific; absence of one template is not itself a finding.

source_concept: Roles and responsibilities for AI risk management are documented and communicated
proposed_assessment_use: Map responsibility for approving, operating, evaluating, monitoring, and retiring AI-enabled workflows.
evidence_examples: role matrices; approval records; operating ownership; escalation paths
adaptation_limit: Formal roles are intent evidence until corroborated by operating examples.

source_concept: Executive leadership takes responsibility for decisions about risks associated with AI system development and deployment
proposed_assessment_use: Ask where material AI risk decisions are escalated and who accepts residual risk.
evidence_examples: governance minutes; approvals; exception/risk acceptance records
adaptation_limit: Do not infer an organizational structure; identify the actual decision forum and authority.

source_concept: Policies and procedures define roles and responsibilities for human-AI configurations and oversight
proposed_assessment_use: Assess whether human review, override, escalation, and accountability are explicit in AI-assisted workflows.
evidence_examples: workflow diagrams; human-review criteria; override procedures; escalation logs
adaptation_limit: Human oversight requirements depend on impact, use case, and user population; this is not a universal staffing prescription.

source_concept: Scientific integrity and TEVV considerations are identified and documented
proposed_assessment_use: Examine whether evaluation design, data collection, and validation methods are fit for the intended AI use.
evidence_examples: evaluation plans; test datasets; validation records; limitations documentation
adaptation_limit: Do not treat a single benchmark score as sufficient evidence of fitness for institutional use.

source_concept: Targeted application scope is specified and documented
proposed_assessment_use: Test whether each AI-enabled use case has a bounded purpose, users, decisions, data, and operating context.
evidence_examples: use-case statement; user groups; data boundaries; exclusions; intended decisions
adaptation_limit: Do not infer production scope from experiments, pilots, or public statements.

source_concept: Processes for human oversight are defined, assessed, and documented
proposed_assessment_use: Assess whether oversight occurs at meaningful points and whether reviewers have enough information and authority to intervene.
evidence_examples: review steps; escalation records; override evidence; user guidance
adaptation_limit: Presence of a human in the loop is not automatically effective oversight.

source_concept: Approaches for mapping risks of third-party software, data, and other components are documented
proposed_assessment_use: Assess dependency and provenance questions for models, APIs, datasets, and other third-party AI components.
evidence_examples: component inventory; provider documentation; data provenance; risk reviews
adaptation_limit: This supports risk assessment, not a recommendation to buy or replace a product.

source_concept: AI system is evaluated for safety
proposed_assessment_use: Ask what safety-relevant failure modes are tested for the actual institutional use case.
evidence_examples: scenario tests; red-team exercises where appropriate; failure analyses; acceptance criteria
adaptation_limit: Safety evidence is use-case specific and cannot be reduced to one generic score.

source_concept: AI system is evaluated for security and resilience
proposed_assessment_use: Assess security/resilience evaluation appropriate to the AI workflow and its dependencies.
evidence_examples: security tests; abuse-case analysis; resilience tests; monitoring results
adaptation_limit: Do not treat AI RMF as a security certification or substitute for system-specific threat assessment.

source_concept: Risks related to transparency and accountability are examined and documented
proposed_assessment_use: Assess whether stakeholders can understand ownership, use, limitations, and accountability for AI-assisted decisions.
evidence_examples: disclosures; responsibility records; user guidance; audit trails
adaptation_limit: Transparency needs vary by audience and decision impact.

source_concept: AI model explanations are explained, validated, and documented
proposed_assessment_use: Ask how explanation or interpretability needs are defined and validated for the actual users and decisions.
evidence_examples: explanation evaluations; user studies; decision-support guidance; limitations
adaptation_limit: Not every use case requires the same explanation technique; fitness is contextual.

source_concept: Privacy risk of the AI system is examined and documented
proposed_assessment_use: Assess how privacy and institutional-data risks are identified in AI workflows.
evidence_examples: data-flow diagrams; privacy reviews; retention rules; access controls
adaptation_limit: The RFQ assessment should surface evidence and questions, not substitute for formal privacy/legal review.

source_concept: Fairness and bias are evaluated and documented
proposed_assessment_use: Ask whether impact-relevant fairness risks and affected groups are identified and evaluated where applicable.
evidence_examples: evaluation plans; subgroup analyses; impact assessments; limitations
adaptation_limit: Applicability and metrics depend on use case and affected population; no universal fairness threshold is implied.

source_concept: Approaches, personnel, and documentation are in place to track identified AI risks over time
proposed_assessment_use: Assess post-deployment or ongoing monitoring of known risks and changes in context.
evidence_examples: risk register; monitoring dashboards; review cadence; drift or performance records
adaptation_limit: Monitoring measures need defined thresholds and response paths; dashboards alone are not evidence of control effectiveness.

source_concept: Whether the AI system achieves intended purposes and whether development or deployment should proceed is determined
proposed_assessment_use: Look for explicit go/no-go or continue/change/stop decisions tied to evidence and intended purpose.
evidence_examples: approval gates; evaluation summaries; decision records; rollback criteria
adaptation_limit: This is a decision structure, not a NIST approval or certification of a system.

source_concept: Responses to identified and measured AI risks are prioritized and documented
proposed_assessment_use: Assess whether material AI risks have owners, treatments, timelines, and residual-risk decisions.
evidence_examples: risk treatments; owners; mitigation tracking; exception decisions
adaptation_limit: Do not compare backlog size across teams without risk and scope context.

source_concept: Procedures are followed to respond to and recover from previously unknown risks when identified
proposed_assessment_use: Assess incident and change pathways for newly discovered AI failure modes or harms.
evidence_examples: incident records; emergency disablement; corrective actions; monitoring changes
adaptation_limit: Avoid assuming an AI-specific incident process is necessary when existing enterprise processes are effective.

source_concept: Mechanisms are in place to supersede, disengage, or deactivate AI systems inconsistent with intended use
proposed_assessment_use: Ask how an AI feature or workflow can be disabled, rolled back, or retired when evidence no longer supports use.
evidence_examples: feature flags; rollback plans; retirement criteria; decommission records
adaptation_limit: Mechanisms vary by architecture; focus on decision and execution capability, not one technical pattern.

source_concept: AI risks and benefits from third-party resources are regularly monitored
proposed_assessment_use: Assess ongoing review of external models, APIs, datasets, and provider changes after initial adoption.
evidence_examples: provider change reviews; model/version inventory; dependency monitoring; updated risk records
adaptation_limit: This is not a vendor ranking or procurement recommendation.
